newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ opposition Labour leader sees leftist linkup.
newsitem.headline: NZ opposition Labour leader sees leftist linkup.

text.p: New Zealand's opposition Labour leader Helen Clark said on Thursday she welcomed signals from the left-wing Alliance grouping that it might join her party in a coalition government after the next election.
Alliance leader Jim Anderton said at the weekend that he was changing tactics to help his grouping to become "part of the positive alternative" to the current centre-right government.

Clark told Reuters in a telephone interview: "The Alliance is now being more explicit about its desire to support or be part of a change of government. It is a logical development under MMP and is to be welcomed as such."

Before the 1996 election, the first held under German-style mixed member proportional (MMP) voting, the Alliance had called for Labour to outline the shape of a coalition before polling day and it refused to strike a deal after the election.

But Labour and the Alliance achieved a new rapport in talks after the election, which resulted in a coalition between Prime Mininster Jim Bolger's conservative National Party and nationalist New Zealand First.

"We had a reasonable agreement with them at the end of the coalition talks and it has moved on from there. As Anderton has said, putting themselves outside having any role in government cost them support. They want to be relevant," Clark said.
Labour's support surged to 45 percent in one recent opinion poll and the party could potentially build a majority centre-left coalition with the Alliance's six percent backing.
The next election is not due unditl 1999, but the ruling coalition has only a one-seat majority in the single-chamber parliament.
Clark said she foresaw a general understanding among the centre-left before an election, but not a detailed programme.

"I don't think there should be a campaign on a common programme. There are areas where there will continue to be significant differences, such as foreign investment, where Labour will continue to favour a reasonably open regime," she said.
She also said there would need to be agreement on a budget strategy but other policy differences could be maintained.

"We should all learn from the mistakes National and New Zealand First have made in putting together a maximalist programme after the election and pretending the parties are of one mind around this programme," she said.

"We should look a bit more widely around the European models and probably go for governmental agreements which do not purport to have the parties in government agreeing on everything, because clearly they don't."
Clark said Labour would accept either a minority government with Alliance support or a majority coalition.
"Given their change of position both options must be on the table. I can personally, and the Labour Party can, live with either," she said.
Clark ruled out a coalition deal with free-market Act, National or NZ First "in its current form".

She also said that despite tensions in NZ First it was unlikely that the current government would fall before 1999. "We know that bad and foolish governments can stagger on. So that has to be a possibility. Probably a strong one," she said.
